Ideological leaning only, the first of Q3's three correlates.
Conspiracy content, Q3's second correlate. With entries 1 and 2 Q3 is stated in full.

The topic-conditioning premise of the method (p.4), which the paper states as a hypothesis it adopts. Related to Q2's methods aim but does not state it; same call as the earlier judge on an equivalent entry.

central_claim.note: Not uniform; varies by place, leaning, topic, and between countries (p.25). Events added, from the abstract.

The conclusion's hedged suggestion that institutional factors 'may' mediate the impact of online polarization on health behavior (p.25), reported with its hedge: the authors' interpretation, in the spirit of F-n1.
The methodological aim (fine-grained text-based measure, adaptable beyond COVID-19, p.3) placed as a central claim.

evidence.note: The three topics and why they were chosen; no conspiracy category or method.
Conspiracy category, counting promotion and rebuttal. Entries 1-4 together give all of E5.
Profile text geocoding with OSM/ArcGIS and census check.
Democrat vs Republican; Canadian left and right party families (p.4). Accurate method detail; the grouping is the source of L8 but is not stated as a limit here.
Validation against voter records (74.35% / 73.35%). With entries 6 and 8, E3 is stated in full.
User-level averaged embeddings, C-index separation of left and right users, 0-1 range. RoBERTa appears in the quote, not the claim; treated as wording.
Subsampling approximation (p.11). Accurate; not in the gold.
Comparison with 2020 U.S. and 2019 Canadian election results: one of E6's three outside sources.
Case and death data and vaccination rates a year later. With entry 12, all three E6 sources.
Daily time series, pre-selected and peak-detected events, event-triggered averaging (p.16, p.19). Accurate method description; not in the gold.

key_findings.note: F1 in full (U.S. masks and vaccines not lockdowns; Canada not significant). Canada's lower overall polarization plus its non-significant association covers F5.
Delaware, Idaho, Alabama, Arkansas exceptions, stated for lockdowns as on p.14 (F6). Quebec highest on vaccines (p.24), not overall and without the English-only caveat: part of F7.
U.S. r = -0.77 and Canada not the same; reports the S3 Fig positive 0.74 (n = 12), which the F2 note accepts. Does not point out the clash with the abstract's 'notably weaker', so no B2 catch.
Rise and fall within days, peaks coinciding with events.
Conservatives 'posted about' conspiracy theories, not endorsed them; U.S. weak negative, Canada not significant.

scope_and_limits.note: Semantic similarity only a proxy that can miss signals (p.24); sarcasm example is given in the next entry.
Sarcasm and indirect disagreement lost in user-level averaging (p.10): the example part of L1.
Party families, Bloc and minor parties excluded.
Self-reported information may be inaccurate (p.24), plus voter-record and name-matching caveats (p.10).
Self-reported locations may be wrong (p.10); VPNs appear only in the quote.

No firm conclusion from the Canadian vaccination correlation, few regions (S3 Fig caption, p.26). Accurate; not in the gold.
The paper's own hedge on event peaks (p.17). Accurate; not a separate gold limit.
No single explanation identified for the conservative-polarization link (p.23). Accurate; not in the gold.
Future-work items from the conclusion (p.26). Accurate; not in the gold.

Extends prior COVID-19 partisanship research with finer geographic and temporal detail.
